narrative: The model estimates a 71% chance that you will leave your job, so the promotion decision treated you as a high retention risk and denied the promotion. The strongest signal was your overall work experience: at 6–10 years, you fall in a range that the model links more strongly to leaving than the larger 1–5 year group among employees predicted to stay. Your tenure in your current organization—1–5 years—also pushed the prediction toward leaving, even though that band is common among stayers; in your profile it still raised the risk. The third most influential factor was that you do not currently have other job opportunities, and this actually pushed toward staying, because lacking outside options usually makes departure less likely. It was not enough to offset the first two signals. Other context—low pay relative to effort, no bonus, no recognition, low emotional commitment, low job stability, and general job dissatisfaction—makes the retention concern understandable, but the decision should not rest only on a leave forecast. Before finalizing denial, the organization should review promotion criteria separately from retention risk, discuss your career path, pay, recognition, and support, and consider a retention plan if it wants to keep you. You should ask for a clear conversation about what would make promotion possible and what concerns are driving this decision.
